summary: Summarizes request-routing techniques that content networks used on or before December 2000 to direct client requests to a suitable server. They fall into DNS, transport-layer, and application-layer methods. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When many servers hold the same website, someone must send you to a good one. This memo lists the ways that was done, such as through the address lookup system or by redirecting at the server.

subtitle: A survey of the ways content networks steered clients to the right server before December 2000.

tldr.problem: When the same content lives on many servers (surrogates), something has to decide which one answers each client request.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sorts the known techniques into DNS request-routing, transport-layer request-routing and application-layer request-routing, and lists the strengths and drawbacks of each.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational survey of techniques in use on or before December 2000, not a standard. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Techniques in use on or before December 2000

today: RFC 3568 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 8996. It is a survey of techniques used on or before December 2000, not a specification.

sections.title: What Request-Routing Is
sections.content:
This memo summarizes request-routing techniques that the industry used before December 2000. Request-routing directs client requests to surrogates based on policies and a possible set of metrics. It is also called content routing or content redirection.

The techniques are commonly used in Content Networks, also known as Content Delivery Networks. A request-routing system may choose a surrogate by network proximity, bandwidth availability, surrogate load and availability of content. The RFC groups the techniques into three classes: DNS, transport-layer and application-layer.
sections.eli5: Imagine many copies of the same library book in different towns. Request-routing is the helper who sends you to the town that can hand you the book fastest.

sections.title: DNS-Based Request-Routing
sections.content:
These techniques are common because of the ubiquity of DNS. A specialized DNS server is inserted into the resolution process and can return a different set of A, NS or CNAME records depending on policy, metrics, or both.

With a single reply, the server returns the address of the best surrogate, which may be a virtual IP address standing for a set of surrogates. With multiple replies, it returns several A records, and common client-side DNS servers cycle through them in round-robin fashion.

Multi-level resolution uses several request-routing DNS servers in one lookup, via NS or CNAME records. NS redirection is limited by the number of parts in the DNS name, lets the last server set the TTL of the whole resolution, and adds delay. CNAME redirection also adds overhead, but the number of request-routing servers does not depend on the format of the domain name.

Object encoding puts the object type or a hash into the DNS name, for example images.a.b.example.com. Object information is then available at resolution time, but the client's DNS server may need multiple resolutions per Web page.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone book that gives different answers to different people. Ask it for a pizza place and it hands you the number of the nearest shop.

sections.title: Anycast and DNS Limitations
sections.content:
With anycast, a request-routing DNS server advertises one anycast address that several physical DNS servers share. The server closest to the client's DNS server in terms of OSPF and BGP routing receives the query and can use that fact in its decision. The RFC lists drawbacks: the DNS server may not be the closest to the client, routing protocols are typically not load sensitive, and server load is not considered.

The RFC also lists general limits of DNS-based routing. DNS only resolves at the domain level, not per object. Short TTL values may be needed to react to outages, which can increase DNS traffic, and many implementations do not honor the TTL. Client addresses are not relayed in DNS requests, so proximity is judged from the client's DNS server. Users sharing one client-site DNS server get the same addresses during the TTL, which can overload a surrogate during a flash crowd.

It also points to RFC 2782 (DNS SRV) for guidance and warnings on using DNS for load balancing.
sections.eli5: DNS can only tell you which shop to visit, not which shelf to look at. It also guesses where you are from the post office you use, not from your home address.

sections.title: Transport-Layer Request-Routing
sections.content:
Here the system inspects the first packet of the client's request. That reveals the client's IP address, port information and layer 4 protocol, which can be combined with policies and metrics to choose a surrogate. The hand-off techniques themselves are beyond the scope of the document.

Forward-flow traffic from the client to the newly selected surrogate flows through the surrogate originally chosen by DNS, while the larger reverse flow typically takes the direct path. The overhead suits long-lived sessions such as FTP and RTSP, and it can also steer clients away from overloaded surrogates. It can be combined with DNS: DNS gives a first step and the transport layer refines it.
sections.eli5: The first greeter looks at who is knocking and passes you to a better-suited helper. The reply then comes straight from that helper.

sections.title: Application-Layer Request-Routing
sections.content:
These systems examine client packets beyond the transport header, which allows control down to individual objects. They know the client's IP address and the requested object.

Header inspection reads hints from HTTP, RTSP or SSL. With URL-based routing, a 302 redirection sends the client from a virtual surrogate to the real delivery node, which is simple but adds latency. An in-path element transparently intercepts the connection, examines the request and splices it to the chosen delivery node, at the cost of URL parsing in the traffic path.

Header-based routing uses fields such as Cookie, Language and User-Agent. Cookies allow client-based service differentiation and session persistence, the language header can select a language-specific node, and the user-agent header can identify device types. Site-specific identifiers such as the SSL Session Identifier can also tie a session to a server.

Content modification, or URL rewriting, lets a content provider rewrite embedded object URLs so clients fetch them from the best surrogate. A-priori rewriting is done before the content is placed on the origin server. On-demand rewriting happens when the request reaches the origin, when the client is known. Limits: the first request must be served by the origin, and rewritten pages should be non-cacheable or cacheable only briefly. Such modification must be consistent with RFC 3238.
sections.eli5: Now the helper reads the whole note you handed over, not just the envelope. It can send you to exactly the right place, or even change the addresses in your note ahead of time.

sections.title: Combining Mechanisms and Measurements
sections.content:
Combinations can beat any single mechanism. DNS can only resolve per domain, but content modification can rewrite references to different objects to point into different domain name spaces, so DNS then directs each object to a different surrogate.

Appendix A covers metrics. Proximity here means round-trip time. Active probing, such as a periodic ICMP ECHO Request to a potential requester, can measure it, but it is periodic, firewalls and NATs disallow probes, and probes often trigger intrusion detection alarms. Metrics include latency, router hop counts and BGP information (AS PATH and MED), though the RFC notes AS PATH can be meaningless as a selection metric. Load feedback can come from probing with an HTTP request or from agents on the surrogates.

The security section says that anyone redirecting requests must address security. When TLS is used, the full URL is not visible to the content network unless it terminates the TLS session.
sections.eli5: Using two tricks together works better than one. One trick picks the town, the other picks the shelf, and the helpers can also check who is least busy.
